analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2017 tax law's lower individual income tax rates permanent.
analysis.headline: Senator Ted Cruz's bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual rate cuts permanent drew no cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax code to keep the individual income tax rates from the 2017 tax law — 10% through 37% — on the books permanently, instead of letting them expire at the end of 2025 as that law scheduled. It would also make the law's new treatment of children's investment income permanent. The cuts are worth the most in dollars to filers with the highest incomes, and making them permanent would come with no way to pay for the lost revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers across income levels keep the lower rates, but the largest dollar savings go to households in the top brackets — the new 37% rate above roughly $500,000 for single filers and $600,000 for couples — and to estates and trusts, which get a permanently lower top rate. Wealthy parents also benefit from permanent rules that tax a child's investment income at preferential brackets for longer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher-income filers, wealthy estates and trusts

how_it_helps.text: Locks in the individual rate brackets from the 2017 tax law (10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37%), which are currently set to revert to higher rates after 2025.
Makes permanent the 2017 law's rules for taxing children's unearned income, which extend the lower brackets to more of a child's investment income.
Sets permanent lower top rates for estates and trusts, with the 37% rate applying above $12,500 of trust income.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately future taxpayers, who would bear the added deficit from making the rate cuts permanent with no offsetting revenue. Since the largest dollar savings go to the highest earners, the cost is spread across everyone while the benefit is concentrated at the top.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offsets, so making the cuts permanent would permanently shrink federal revenue; the 2017 law's authors set the individual rates to expire in 2025 precisely to limit the official ten-year cost.

The rate structure it locks in delivers the largest savings in dollars to the top brackets, and the kiddie-tax provisions it makes permanent primarily benefit families with significant investment income for their children.
Permanence means the cuts cannot simply lapse if deficits or later fiscal needs require it; Congress would have to affirmatively raise rates instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Everyone who files taxes would keep somewhat lower rates, which is a real benefit to ordinary filers. But the bill is designed so that the biggest dollar gains go to the top brackets and to trusts and estates, and it provides no way to pay for itself — so the cost is deferred to future taxpayers and to federal borrowing. A permanence-only bill, with none of the temporary middle-class provisions extended alongside it and no offsets, tilts clearly toward concentrated benefit at a diffuse public cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on January 4, 2018, the day after the new session began.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance; that referral was the only action the bill ever received.
Under the 2017 tax law the bill targeted, the individual rates are scheduled to expire and revert to higher rates at the end of 2025; the bill would have removed that expiration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one got anything from the bill itself. Because it died, the scheduled 2025 expiration of the rate cuts remains on the books, and future taxpayers avoided a permanent, unpaid-for revenue loss whose largest dollar benefits would have gone to the highest earners. Middle-income households also lost nothing they currently have, since the existing rates were already law through 2025.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Future taxpayers who'd have borne the deficits

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill or scheduled any action on it

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The only senator who put his name on the bill was a Republican, and no other member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would permanently keep the 37% top rate and the full TCJA rate structure, whose largest dollar savings go to filers above the $500,000–$600,000 thresholds. The cost — lost federal revenue with no offsets — is spread across everyone else and future taxpayers.
Trust income above $12,500 would be taxed at a permanent 37% top rate instead of reverting to 39.6%. Wealthy families that hold assets in trusts benefit directly.
The bill makes permanent the kiddie-tax rules that keep more of a child's unearned income in lower brackets, a benefit concentrated among affluent families shifting investment income to children.
Making the rate cuts permanent with no pay-for would permanently reduce federal revenue, adding to deficits and squeezing future budget room for public priorities.
